title: How do you resolve merge conflicts, and how do you undo a bad commit that has already been pushed to a shared branch (`git revert` vs `reset` + force-push, and why `revert` on shared history)?
shortTitle: Resolving merge conflicts and undoing a bad commit already pushed to a shared branch (revert vs reset + force-push)

s1_definition.profdef: A merge conflict occurs when Git cannot automatically reconcile two branches because the same lines of a file were changed differently on each side; you resolve it by opening the conflicted files, choosing or combining the changes, marking them resolved, and completing the merge. To undo a bad commit that is already pushed to a shared branch, you use `git revert`, which creates a new commit that inverts the bad change, preserving history. You do not use `git reset` plus a force-push on shared branches, because that rewrites history everyone else has already pulled, causing divergence and lost work for teammates. Reset with force-push is only safe on private, unshared branches.
s1_definition.analogy: A merge conflict is like two tellers at the National Bank of India both editing the same line of the same account's instructions at the same time — one writes "limit 50000" and the other writes "limit 75000," and the system cannot guess which is right, so it stops and asks a human to decide. Undoing a mistake that is already shared is the important part: if a wrong entry was already copied into every branch's ledger, you do not secretly erase it and pretend it never happened, because every branch still has the old copy and chaos follows. Instead you make a new, clearly-dated correcting entry that cancels the mistake — everyone can see what happened and everyone stays in sync. Secretly erasing is only acceptable in your own private notebook that nobody else has copied.
s1_definition.oneliner: Resolve conflicts by choosing or combining the clashing lines and completing the merge; undo a pushed commit with `git revert` which adds an inverting commit, never with `reset` plus force-push on a shared branch because that rewrites history others already have.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A merge conflict occurs when Git cannot automatically reconcile two branches because the same lines of a file were changed differently on each side; you resolve it by opening the conflicted files, choosing or combining the changes, marking them resolved, and completing the merge. To undo a bad commit that is already pushed to a shared branch, you use `git revert`, which creates a new commit that inverts the bad change, preserving history. You do not use `git reset` plus a force-push on shared branches, because that rewrites history everyone else has already pulled, causing divergence and lost work for teammates. Reset with force-push is only safe on private, unshared branches.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A merge conflict is like two tellers at the National Bank of India both editing the same line of the same account's instructions at the same time — one writes "limit 50000" and the other writes "limit 75000," and the system cannot guess which is right, so it stops and asks a human to decide. Undoing a mistake that is already shared is the important part: if a wrong entry was already copied into every branch's ledger, you do not secretly erase it and pretend it never happened, because every branch still has the old copy and chaos follows. Instead you make a new, clearly-dated correcting entry that cancels the mistake — everyone can see what happened and everyone stays in sync. Secretly erasing is only acceptable in your own private notebook that nobody else has copied.

**One line to remember:** Resolve conflicts by choosing or combining the clashing lines and completing the merge; undo a pushed commit with `git revert` which adds an inverting commit, never with `reset` plus force-push on a shared branch because that rewrites history others already have.

sections.s2_technical:
A merge conflict happens when two branches changed the same region of a file in incompatible ways, so Git cannot decide automatically. When you merge or rebase and hit a conflict, Git pauses and marks the conflicted files with conflict markers: the section between `<<<<<<<` and `=======` is your current branch's version, and the section between `=======` and `>>>>>>>` is the incoming version. You resolve by editing the file to the correct final content — keeping one side, the other, or a combination — then removing the markers, staging the file with `git add`, and completing the operation with `git commit` for a merge or `git rebase --continue` for a rebase. Good practice is to understand both changes before choosing, use a three-way merge tool for complex conflicts, run the tests after resolving because a syntactically clean resolution can still be logically wrong, and keep branches short-lived and frequently integrated so conflicts stay small. If a merge goes badly you can abort with `git merge --abort` and start over.

Undoing commits splits into two very different situations, and the distinction is the whole point of the question. If the bad commit is only in your local, unshared branch — nobody else has pulled it — you can rewrite history freely. `git reset` moves the branch pointer backward: a soft reset keeps your changes staged, a mixed reset keeps them in the working directory unstaged, and a hard reset discards them entirely. Rewriting local history is fine because no one else is affected.

The moment a commit is pushed to a shared branch that teammates have pulled, the rules change. The bad commit is now part of history that other clones depend on. If you `git reset` to before it and force-push, you rewrite the shared history: the remote branch now has a different set of commits, and every teammate who already pulled the old history is now divergent. Their next pull conflicts or, worse, they re-push the old commits and the "deleted" bad commit comes back, and work can be silently lost. This is why you never reset-and-force-push a shared branch.

The correct tool is `git revert`. Revert does not delete the bad commit; it creates a brand new commit that applies the exact inverse of the bad commit's changes, cancelling its effect while leaving the original in history. Because revert only adds a commit and never rewrites existing history, everyone can pull it normally with no divergence, and the audit trail clearly shows both the mistake and its correction — which in a bank is often a compliance requirement. You revert with `git revert <commit>`, and for a merge commit you specify the parent to keep with `-m 1`. A senior nuance: force-pushing to a shared branch is acceptable only in narrow, coordinated cases, such as a personal feature branch that is genuinely yours, and even then teams prefer `git push --force-with-lease` which refuses to overwrite if someone else pushed in the meantime, preventing you from clobbering a teammate's work. Protected main and release branches should have force-push disabled in the server settings precisely to make this mistake impossible. The guiding principle is: rewrite private history freely, but on shared history only ever move forward with new commits.
sections.s3_banking:
A developer at the National Bank of India pushed a commit to the shared development branch that broke the transfer fee calculation for Rajesh and Priya. Teammates have already pulled it. The developer must undo it safely.

Problem 1 — While merging a feature, the developer hits a merge conflict in the fee-calculation file because two branches changed the same line. They must resolve it by choosing the correct final content and completing the merge.

Problem 2 — A bad commit is already on the shared development branch and teammates have it. The developer is tempted to reset and force-push, which would rewrite shared history and break everyone's clones. The system must reject that approach.

Problem 3 — The correct action is a revert that adds an inverting commit, which everyone can pull normally and which preserves the audit trail required in banking.

Our runnable Java simulation models a `SharedBranch` with commits pulled by multiple clones, a `ConflictResolver` that detects and resolves a line conflict, and a `HistoryEditor` that refuses a reset-force-push on a shared branch and instead performs a safe revert. Classes: `Commit`, `SharedBranch`, `ConflictResolver`, `HistoryEditor`, and an `UndoDemo` main.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -cp target/classes com.bank.vcs.UndoDemo

# Resolve a real conflict:
git merge feature/fee-update          # hits conflict
# edit FeeCalculator.java, remove <<<<<<< ======= >>>>>>> markers, keep correct content
git add FeeCalculator.java
git commit                            # completes the merge
# (or 'git merge --abort' to start over)

# Undo a BAD commit already pushed to SHARED 'development' (SAFE):
git revert <bad-sha>                  # creates an inverting commit, history moves forward
git push                              # everyone pulls normally, no divergence

# reset + force-push is ONLY for a PRIVATE branch nobody pulled:
git reset --hard <good-sha>
git push --force-with-lease           # refuses if a teammate pushed meanwhile
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a merge that produces a line conflict in the fee calculator, and a shared development branch that already contains a bad commit pulled by four teammates.

Step 1: The merge hits a conflict because two branches changed the same fee-rate line differently — one side set the rate to 0.001 and the other to 0.0015. Git pauses and marks the file with the ours and theirs sections. The resolver picks the compliance-approved 0.0015 rate as the final content, the markers are removed, the file is staged, and the merge is completed.

Step 2: Attention turns to the bad commit on the shared development branch. The branch history has the base commit and the bad fee-calculation commit, and four teammate clones have already pulled that history, so the branch is shared.

Step 3: The developer is tempted to reset the branch back to before the bad commit and force-push. The history editor refuses this outright because the branch is shared — rewriting history that four clones already have would make all of them diverge and risk silently losing work when they next push or pull.

Step 4: Because reset-force-push was refused, the developer performs the correct action, a revert. This adds a new commit that applies the exact inverse of the bad commit, cancelling its broken rounding while leaving the original bad commit in history. Everyone can pull this new commit normally with no divergence.

Step 5: The final shared history is forward-only: base commit, bad commit, and the revert commit. The audit trail clearly shows both the mistake and its correction, which satisfies banking compliance, and no teammate's clone was disrupted.

```

2026-10-30 03:11:30 [WARNING]   =======
2026-10-30 03:11:30 [WARNING]   >>>>>>> theirs: fee = amount.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.0015"));
2026-10-30 03:11:30 [INFO   ] Resolved by choosing: fee = amount.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.0015")); // compliance-approved rate  (markers removed, git add, commit)
2026-10-30 03:11:30 [SEVERE ] REFUSED: reset+force-push on SHARED branch 'development' — 4 clones already pulled this history. Rewriting it would diverge everyone and risk lost work.
2026-10-30 03:11:30 [INFO   ] git revert c2 -> new commit c3 (bad change inverted, original kept in history, everyone pulls normally)
2026-10-30 03:11:30 [INFO   ] Final shared history (forward-only, audit preserved):
2026-10-30 03:11:30 [INFO   ]   c1 transfer-service base

2026-10-30 03:11:30 [INFO   ]   c3 Revert "fee calc (BROKEN rounding for SAV2001/CUR3001)"
```

```
  ═══ LLD — Conflict Resolve + History Editor (National Bank of India) ═══

  │ + resolve(ours,theirs,chosen) │                    │ owns ◆ *

                                            │          Commit          │
                                            │ - id / message / isRevert│
                                            └──────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Undo Decision ──────────────────────────────────

  [BAD COMMIT PUSHED] ──branch shared?──→ yes → [REVERT] (forward-only)
                               │
                               └── no (private) → [RESET + force-with-lease]

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────────────

  1. resolver.resolve(ours, theirs, chosen)   → conflict fixed
  2. dev.pulledByClones(4)                     → branch is shared
  3. editor.resetAndForcePush(dev, "c1")       → REFUSED (shared)
  4. editor.revert(dev, bad)                   → c3 inverting commit
  5. history = c1 → c2 → c3   forward-only, audit intact
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A merge conflict happens when two branches changed the same region of a file in incompatible ways, so Git cannot decide automatically and pauses, marking the file with conflict markers where the section between the less-than signs and the equals signs is my current branch's version and the section between the equals signs and the greater-than signs is the incoming version. I resolve it by understanding both changes, editing the file to the correct final content — keeping one side, the other, or a combination — removing the markers, staging with git add, and completing the merge with a commit or a rebase continue. I always run the tests afterward, because a resolution that compiles can still be logically wrong, and I keep branches short-lived so conflicts stay small; if it goes badly I abort and start over.

Undoing commits depends entirely on whether the commit is shared. If it is only in my local branch that nobody else has pulled, I can rewrite history freely with git reset, because no one else is affected. But the moment a commit is pushed to a shared branch that teammates have pulled, the rules change completely. If I reset to before it and force-push, I rewrite the shared history, and every teammate who already pulled the old history diverges — their next pull conflicts, work can be silently lost, and the deleted commit can even come back when someone re-pushes. That is why I never reset-and-force-push a shared branch.

The correct tool for shared history is git revert, which does not delete the bad commit but creates a brand new commit that applies its exact inverse, cancelling the effect while leaving the original in history. Because revert only moves history forward and never rewrites it, everyone pulls it normally with no divergence, and the audit trail clearly shows both the mistake and the correction, which in a bank is often a compliance requirement. In my project at the National Bank of India, a teammate pushed a commit to the shared development branch that broke the transfer fee rounding for customers like Rajesh and Priya, and four of us had already pulled it. Resetting and force-pushing would have broken everyone's clones, so I used git revert to add an inverting commit that everyone could pull cleanly, preserving the full history. The nuance I always add is that force-pushing is acceptable only on a genuinely private branch, and even then I use force-with-lease so I cannot clobber a teammate's work, and we disable force-push on protected branches entirely. The principle I always state is rewrite private history freely, but on shared history only ever move forward with new commits.
